summary: With the psrp connection plugin, matching the PSRemoting session configuration to ansible_pwsh_interpreter avoids spawning a new PowerShell process per task. Set ansible_psrp_configuration_name to Microsoft.PowerShell (5.1, default) or PowerShell.7, and list configurations with Get-PSSessionConfiguration.
questions: Why are my psrp tasks slow after switching to PowerShell 7?
How do I make psrp use the PowerShell 7 session configuration?
How do I list PSRemoting session configurations on a Windows host?
When is the PowerShell.7 session configuration registered?

answer_card.title: Matching the PSRP session configuration to PowerShell 7
answer_card.answer_md:
With `ansible.builtin.psrp`, if the PSRemoting session configuration doesn't match `ansible_pwsh_interpreter`, PSRP has to start a new PowerShell process for every task, which slows playbooks. Match them with `ansible_psrp_configuration_name`:
- `Microsoft.PowerShell` (default): Windows PowerShell 5.1
- `PowerShell.7`: PowerShell 7

PowerShell 7 registers `PowerShell.7` during install (if that option is selected) or when you run `Enable-PSRemoting` from PowerShell 7.

```ini
[windows:vars]
ansible_connection=psrp
ansible_pwsh_interpreter=C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe
ansible_psrp_configuration_name=PowerShell.7
```

List available configurations on the host:

```powershell
Get-PSSessionConfiguration | Select-Object Name, PSVersion
```
